title: Security Hardening
description: Apply Linux security hardening techniques including SSH lockdown, firewall rules, user permissions, and kernel hardening.

data.text: Security hardening reduces the attack surface of your Linux servers. The goal is not to make systems impenetrable, but to make attacks expensive, noisy, and unlikely to succeed.
This lesson covers SSH restrictions, firewall configuration, user privilege controls, and kernel-level hardening that any engineer can apply without specialized security knowledge.
SSH is the most common entry point for attackers. A few configuration changes in sshd_config drastically reduce brute-force and credential theft risks.

items: Use key-based authentication only: PasswordAuthentication no
Change the default port as an obscurity layer: Port 2222
Enable two-factor authentication for privileged users

data.title: Hardened sshd_config snippet
data.code:
Port 2222
PermitRootLogin no
PasswordAuthentication no
PubkeyAuthentication yes
AllowUsers deploy admin
MaxAuthTries 3
ClientAliveInterval 300
ClientAliveCountMax 2

# Restart sshd after changes
sudo systemctl restart sshd

data.title: Watch Out
data.text: Never enable PasswordAuthentication unless you also enforce strong passwords and rate limiting. Key-based authentication is significantly more secure and easier to audit.
`ufw` simplifies `iptables` for common server scenarios. Start by denying everything, then allow only the ports your services actually need.

data.title: Basic ufw firewall setup
data.code:
sudo ufw default deny incoming
sudo ufw default allow outgoing
sudo ufw allow 2222/tcp      # SSH
sudo ufw allow 80/tcp        # HTTP
sudo ufw allow 443/tcp       # HTTPS
sudo ufw enable
sudo ufw status verbose

data.text: Run services as dedicated users with minimal permissions. Use `sudo` instead of root, and enable kernel hardening parameters that mitigate common exploitation techniques.

items: Create service-specific users with no login shell: /usr/sbin/nologin
Set umask to 027 to restrict default file permissions
Use fail2ban to block repeated failed logins
Audit SSH access and disable password authentication
Enable ufw with a default deny policy
Run services as dedicated users, not root
Install fail2ban and configure SSH jails
Review kernel hardening settings with sysctl

data.title: Summary
data.text: Security hardening is a layered practice. Harden SSH, restrict traffic with a firewall, minimize user privileges, and tune kernel protections. Each layer slows attackers and gives you more time to detect and respond.
